title: Stocking the Shelves and the Storm
goal: I can use equal groups, arrays and repeated addition to multiply, and I can trace a chain of causes and effects in a story.

card.desc: You help Mia trace the storm in the stockroom, one cause and effect at a time, from a loose shutter all the way to less inventory for opening day. Then you stock Grandpa's shelves with equal groups and arrays, and turn repeated addition into multiplication (5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 4 × 5 = 20) (Pathways Week 6). Light work over the next two weeks, then Lesson 7 right after Christmas.

win: You traced the whole storm chain and stocked the shelves with equal groups. Grandpa's trading post is ready!

slides.title: Stocking the Shelves and the Storm
slides.text:
Grandpa's trading post opens soon. Today you help in two ways.
You find out why the stockroom got wet.
Then you learn a fast way to count equal groups. 🛒⛈️

notes.do: Before class: about 40 counters (beans or cubes), 6 small paper cups, 10 index cards, whiteboard and 2 marker colors, pencil. Open this class lesson with code 9110 on the library table so you both see the screen.
notes.say: Today has two parts. First, a story about a storm and everything it caused. Then math: a fast way to count groups that are the same size.
notes.ask: Have you ever seen one small thing cause a big mess?
notes.listen: Any real example (a cup tipped over, the dog knocked something down). Praise it: that is cause and effect, today's reading skill.

slides.title: Remember Weeks 1 to 4
slides.text: Four quick ones from your fall lessons.

items.q: Round 562 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: 562 is between 500 and 600. The tens digit is 6. 6 is 5 or more, so round up to 600.
items.no: Look at the tens digit. Is it 5 or more?
items.hint: The tens digit is 6. Round up.

items.q: Which one is true?
items.why: Both have 5 hundreds. 570 has 7 tens. 507 has 0 tens. So 570 > 507.
no: 507 has 0 tens. 570 has 7 tens. So 507 is the smaller one.
The digits are in different places, so they are not equal.

items.why: 6 + 8 = 14: write 4, regroup 1 ten. 5 + 7 + 1 = 13 tens: write 3, regroup 1 hundred. 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. 434.
items.no: Line up the ones, tens and hundreds. Did you regroup two times?

items.q: A story ends: Being honest is always best. That big lesson is the story's ____.
items.why: The lesson a story teaches is the theme.
items.no: It is the big lesson of the story. It starts with th.

notes.do: She answers out loud first, then types or taps. These are Weeks 1–4 skills from her Checkpoint, so they stay fresh over the holidays.
notes.listen: 600, 570 > 507, 434, theme. If she gets 424 or 334 for 256 + 178, she lost a regrouped ten or hundred: have her write it in columns on the whiteboard.

slides.title: The Storm in the Stockroom
slides.text: Read Mia's story with Mr. Jonathan. Take turns, one line each.

visual.text:
A big storm hit Grandpa's trading post at night.
In the morning, Mia found puddles on the stockroom floor. The room smelled musty.
Mia wanted to know why. She looked around like a detective.
She traced the puddles back to a loose shutter on the stockroom window.
The shutter cracked in the wind. Rain got inside. The boxes got soaked. The wet boxes collapsed (fell down). The goods spilled and were ruined.
Now the store has less inventory for opening day. (Inventory means all the things a store has to sell.)
Theo boarded up the broken shutter.

prompts: What did Mia find in the morning?
Why did Mia act like a detective?
What was the first thing that went wrong? What was the last?
starters: The first thing was … The last thing was …

notes.do: 6 minutes. Take turns reading lines aloud. On the whiteboard, draw a puddle and write WHY? next to it.
notes.say: Mia saw a problem and asked WHY. That is what good readers do with cause and effect.
notes.ask: What was the very first thing that went wrong? What was the very last?
notes.listen: First: the loose shutter. Last: less inventory for opening day. If she says the puddles, say: the puddles are what Mia SAW first. Did something happen before the puddles? Check that she knows inventory = the things a store has to sell.

slides.title: Reading words
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word. Then say what it means in your own words.

words.meaning: The reason why something happens.
words.example: The storm was the cause of the puddles.

words.meaning: What happens because of a cause.
words.example: Puddles on the floor were an effect of the storm.

words.meaning: Effects in a row. Each one causes the next one.
words.example: Falling dominoes are a chain reaction.

words.meaning: A result of an action. It is often a bad result.
words.example: Ruined goods were a consequence of the wet boxes.

words.meaning: To follow a chain back to where it started.
words.example: Mia traced the puddles back to the shutter.

notes.do: Flip each card. She reads the word and meaning, then says it in her own words. Write CAUSE and EFFECT big on two index cards; you hold them up on the next slides.
notes.ask: Which word answers WHY? Which word answers WHAT HAPPENED?
notes.listen: Cause = why. Effect = what happened. Pathways asks her to TYPE cause, effect and trace, so have her spell consequence and trace out loud too.

slides.title: Why? What happened?
slides.text:
A cause is why something happens.
An effect is what happens.
The cause always happens first.

steps.text: Storm at night ➡️ puddles on the floor. The storm is the cause. The puddles are the effect.
To find a cause, ask: Why did this happen?
To find an effect, ask: What happened because of this?
Clue words like because and so can help. Some stories do not use them. You can still ask why.

slides.tip: Mia saw the puddles first. But the storm still happened first.

notes.do: Hold up the CAUSE card in your left hand and the EFFECT card in your right. Reveal one step at a time.
notes.say: A story can tell the effect first. Mia saw the puddles first. But the cause still happened first in time.
notes.ask: The stockroom smelled musty. Is the smell a cause or an effect? What caused it?
notes.listen: Effect. The water from the storm caused it. If she says cause, ask: did the smell make the water, or did the water make the smell?

slides.title: Cause or effect?
slides.text: Read the sentence. Look at the bold part. Is it the cause or the effect? Tap a card. Then tap a box.

items.text: The dog ran through the mud, so the rug got dirty.
items.why: The mud is why the rug got dirty.
items.hint: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

items.text: The dog ran through the mud, so the rug got dirty.
items.why: A dirty rug is what happened.
items.hint: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

items.text: Nia forgot her umbrella, so she got wet.
items.why: Forgetting the umbrella is why she got wet.

items.text: The milk spilled because the cup tipped over.
items.why: The cup tipped first. That is why the milk spilled.
items.hint: The word because comes right before the cause.

items.text: Because the bus was late, Sam missed the bell.
items.why: Missing the bell is what happened because the bus was late.
items.hint: What happened first: the late bus, or the missed bell?

items.text: The ice melted because the sun came out.
items.why: The sun came out first. The ice melting is what happened.
items.hint: The word because comes right before the cause.

slides.done: Ask why? to find the cause. Ask what happened? to find the effect.

notes.do: She reads each sentence aloud and asks both questions before she taps. Point at your CAUSE and EFFECT cards as she decides.
notes.ask: In 'The milk spilled because the cup tipped over', which happened first?
notes.listen: The cup tipped first, so it is the cause even though it comes second in the sentence. That is the sentence that trips readers up.

slides.title: Mia's storm chain
slides.text: Tap the events in the order they happened.
steps: The shutter cracked in the wind.
The goods spilled and were ruined.
There was less inventory for opening day.
slides.why: Each event caused the next one. That is a chain reaction.
slides.hint: Not yet. Ask: what had to happen before this?

notes.do: Hands-on first: she writes each event on an index card in short words (loose, cracked, rain in, soaked, collapsed, ruined, less to sell) and lines them up on the table with arrows between them. Then she taps the order on screen.
notes.say: Each card pushes the next one, like a row of dominoes.
notes.ask: Take away the 'rain got inside' card. Can the boxes still get soaked?
notes.listen: No. If one step is missing, the chain breaks. Keep the cards on the table for the next slide.

slides.title: One event, two jobs
slides.text:
In the middle of a chain, an event has two jobs.
It is an effect of what came before.
It is a cause of what comes next.

visual.text: rain got inside ➡️ boxes got soaked ➡️ boxes collapsed

steps.text: Look back: What caused this? Rain got inside.
Look ahead: What did this cause? The boxes collapsed.
The first event is only a cause. The last event is only an effect.

slides.tip: Middle events are both a cause and an effect.

notes.do: Point to her 'soaked' card. Touch the card before it, then the card after it.
notes.ask: 'The goods spilled and were ruined.' What caused it? What did it cause?
notes.listen: Caused by the boxes collapsing. It caused less inventory for opening day. So it is both.

slides.title: Trace a new chain
slides.text: Read this new story. Then answer.

visual.text: Kayla left her crayons on the hot car seat. The crayons melted. The wax dripped on the seat. Mom had to scrub the seat. They were late for the game.

items.q: What was the first cause?
choices: Mom had to scrub the seat.
They were late for the game.
items.why: Everything started when Kayla left the crayons on the hot seat.
no: The crayons melted because of something that happened before.
That happened near the end of the chain.
That is the very last effect.

items.q: The crayons melted. Is that a cause, an effect, or both? Type cause, effect or both.
items.why: It is an effect of the hot seat. It is the cause of the dripping wax. It is both.
items.no: Ask two questions: What caused it? What did it cause?

items.q: What was the last effect?
choices: The wax dripped on the seat.
Mom had to scrub the seat.
Kayla left her crayons on the seat.
They were late for the game.
items.why: Scrubbing took time, so they were late for the game. Nothing comes after that.
no: The wax dripping caused something else.
Scrubbing the seat caused one more thing.
That is the first cause, not the last effect.

notes.do: She reads the story aloud, then draws the chain on the whiteboard with arrows before she answers.
notes.ask: Why were they late for the game? Trace it all the way back.
notes.listen: Kayla left the crayons, both, late for the game. Tracing back: late ← scrubbing ← wax dripped ← crayons melted ← left on the hot seat.

slides.title: Reading check
slides.text: On your own. No looking back!

items.q: Who looked for the cause of the puddles?
items.why: Mia traced the puddles back to the loose shutter.
items.no: She found the puddles in the morning.

items.q: Mia found the problem. Then who put boards over the shutter?
items.why: Theo boarded up the shutter.
items.no: Mia found the problem. Who fixed it?

items.q: Mia followed the puddles back. Where did the chain start?
items.why: Mia traced it back to a loose shutter.
no: The puddles are what she saw. Something came before them.
The soaked boxes are in the middle of the chain.
The ruined goods came near the end.

items.q: Mia started at the puddles. She went back, step by step, to the start of the chain. The word for this is ____.
items.why: To trace a chain is to follow it back to the start.
items.no: Mia did this with the puddles. It starts with tr.

notes.do: On her own. Note her first answers.
notes.listen: Mia, Theo, a loose shutter, trace. If she mixes up Mia and Theo, say: Mia found it, Theo fixed it.

slides.title: Math words
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word. Then spell array and product out loud.

words.meaning: To put equal groups together fast.
words.example: 3 groups of 4? Multiply: 3 × 4 = 12.

words.meaning: Groups with the same number in each one.
words.example: 3 bags with 5 nuts in each bag are equal groups.

words.meaning: Adding the same number again and again.
words.example: 5 + 5 + 5 is repeated addition.

words.meaning: Things set in equal rows and columns.
words.example: 2 rows of 6 cans make an array.

words.meaning: The answer when you multiply.
words.example: In 3 × 4 = 12, the product is 12.

notes.do: Flip each card. She reads it. Then she spells array and product out loud while you write them on the whiteboard. Pathways asks her to TYPE these words.
notes.listen: 10. If she says 5 or 2, say: those are the numbers we multiply. The product is the answer.

slides.title: Grandpa's lanterns
slides.text: Grandpa has 5 crates. He puts 3 lanterns in each crate. Make the groups.
slides.hint: Each crate is one group. Set Groups to the number of crates. Set In each group to the lanterns in one crate.

notes.do: Hands-on first: 5 paper cups, 3 counters in each. She skip counts by 3s while touching each cup: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Then she builds it on screen.
notes.ask: Are the groups equal? How do you know?
notes.listen: Yes, every cup has 3. If she counts every counter by ones, model the skip count once, then have her do it.

slides.title: Add it, or multiply it
slides.text:
When groups are equal, you can add the same number again and again.
Or you can multiply. You get the same answer.

steps.text: Count the groups: 4. Count in one group: 5.

slides.tip: Number of groups × number in each group = the product.

notes.do: Write 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 on the whiteboard. Under it, write 4 × 5. Circle the 4 (how many groups) and the 5 (how many in each).
notes.say: Multiplication is a shortcut for adding the same number again and again.
notes.ask: How many 5s did we add? So what is the first number?
notes.listen: Four 5s, so 4 × 5. If she writes 5 × 4, it is still 20 (turn-around fact), but have her say '4 groups of 5'.

slides.title: Add or multiply
slides.text: Use counters or draw circles if it helps.

items.q: Write 6 + 6 + 6 as multiplication: ____
items.no: Count how many 6s you see. That is the number of groups.

items.q: 2 × 7 means 7 + 7. What is 2 × 7?
items.no: 2 groups of 7. Add 7 + 7.

items.q: Which addition matches 4 × 3?
no: 4 + 3 = 7. That adds 4 and 3 only one time.
That is four 4s, or 16.
That is only three 3s, or 9.

items.q: Jo has 3 bags. They have 4, 5 and 4 nuts. Are they equal groups? Type equal or not equal.
items.why: One bag has 5. The groups are not equal, so Jo must add: 4 + 5 + 4 = 13.
items.no: Look at each bag. Do they all have the same number?

notes.do: She builds each one with counters or draws circles on the whiteboard before she answers.
notes.ask: Why can't Jo multiply to find the total?
notes.listen: 3 × 6 (6 × 3 is fine too), 14, 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, not equal. Multiplying only works when every group is the same size.

slides.title: Arrays: rows and columns
slides.text:
An array puts things in equal rows.
Rows go across ➡️. Columns go up and down ⬇️.

steps.text: Count how many in one row: 6.
Multiply rows × how many in each row: 4 × 6 = 24.

notes.do: Hands-on: she builds 4 rows of 6 counters on the table. Then turn the paper a quarter turn: now it is 6 rows of 4. Same counters.
notes.say: Turn an array and the product stays the same: 4 × 6 and 6 × 4 are both 24.
notes.ask: Which number tells how many rows?
notes.listen: The first number, 4. Watch that she counts rows across, not columns.

items.q: This array has 2 rows of 9. How many baskets in all?
items.no: Add one row of 9 to another row of 9.

items.q: Which fact matches this array?
items.why: 5 rows with 3 in each row: 5 × 3 = 15.
no: 5 + 3 = 8. There are more than 8 candles.
Each row has 3, not 5.
There are 5 rows, not 3.

items.q: An array has 3 rows. Each row has 4 lanterns. 3 × 4 = ____
items.no: Skip count by 4s three times.

notes.do: She touches each row on the screen and skip counts out loud.
notes.listen: 18, 5 × 3, 12. If she picks 5 + 3, she is adding the two numbers instead of multiplying: build it with counters.

slides.title: Math check
slides.text: On your own. Use counters or draw if you need to.

items.q: Grandpa fills 3 shelves. Each shelf has 6 boxes. How many boxes?
items.no: Each shelf is a group. Skip count by 6s, once for each shelf.

items.q: In 6 × 3 = 18, the 18 is called the ____.
items.why: The answer when you multiply is the product.
items.no: It is the answer to a times fact. It starts with p.

items.q: Mia puts 2 rows of 8 seed packets on a shelf. How many packets?
no: That is 2 + 8. Two rows of 8 is 8 + 8.
Count again: 8 + 8 = 16.
82 just puts the digits side by side.

items.q: Write 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 as multiplication: ____
items.no: Count the 3s. That is the number of groups.

notes.do: On her own. Note her first answers.
notes.listen: 18, product, 16, 6 × 3 (3 × 6 is fine). If she counts the six 3s wrong, have her touch each one.

slides.title: Two big skills
slides.text:
Reading: cause ➡️ effect ➡️ effect. Ask why? and what happened next?
Math: equal groups ➡️ multiply. Groups × how many in each.
slides.tip: Your work for the next two weeks is light. Read your list with Mr. Jonathan!

notes.do: Open the course page. Read the task list with her, one line at a time. Show her the optional Winter holiday lesson. Remind her to bring packet page 2 on Dec 29.
notes.say: You worked hard this fall. Your next lesson is Tuesday, December 29, right after Christmas.
notes.ask: Tell me one cause and effect from your own day.
notes.listen: Any true pair, said as 'Because …, …' or '…, so …'.

slides.title: On Your Own: Shelves and Storms
slides.text: You learned two big skills in class. Now try them on your own. Take your time. 🛒⛈️

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: What is a cause? What is an effect?
In Mia's stockroom, what was the first thing that went wrong?
starters: A cause is … An effect is …

slides.title: Your 10 words
slides.text: Tap each card. Say the word. Say what it means.

words.meaning: The reason why something happens.
words.example: The storm was the cause of the puddles.

words.meaning: What happens because of a cause.
words.example: Puddles on the floor were an effect of the storm.

words.meaning: Effects in a row. Each one causes the next one.
words.example: Falling dominoes are a chain reaction.

words.meaning: A result of an action. It is often a bad result.
words.example: Ruined goods were a consequence of the wet boxes.

words.meaning: To follow a chain back to where it started.
words.example: Mia traced the puddles back to the shutter.

words.meaning: To put equal groups together fast.
words.example: 3 groups of 4? Multiply: 3 × 4 = 12.

words.meaning: Groups with the same number in each one.
words.example: 3 bags with 5 nuts in each bag are equal groups.

words.meaning: Adding the same number again and again.
words.example: 5 + 5 + 5 is repeated addition.

words.meaning: Things set in equal rows and columns.
words.example: 2 rows of 6 cans make an array.

words.meaning: The answer when you multiply.
words.example: In 3 × 4 = 12, the product is 12.

slides.title: Cause and effect chains
slides.text:
Ask why? to find the cause. Ask what happened? to find the effect.
In a chain, each effect causes the next thing.

visual.text: loose shutter ➡️ shutter cracked ➡️ rain got inside ➡️ boxes got soaked ➡️ boxes collapsed ➡️ goods ruined ➡️ less inventory

slides.tip: Middle events are both a cause and an effect.

slides.title: Cause or effect?
slides.text: Look at the bold part.

items.q: The wind blew hard, so the hat flew away. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
items.why: The wind is why the hat flew away. It is the cause.
items.no: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

items.q: The oven was too hot, so the cookies burned. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
items.why: Burned cookies are what happened. It is the effect.
items.no: Which happened first: the hot oven or the burned cookies?

items.q: Jada studied every night. She got 100 on her test. Which part is the effect?
items.why: Getting 100 is what happened because she studied.
no: Studying is why she got 100. That is the cause.
The story does not say that.

slides.title: Max's sticky morning
slides.text: Max had a bad morning. Tap what happened, in order.
steps: The juice ran onto his homework.
He had to write it again.
slides.why: Each event caused the next one. That is a chain reaction.
slides.hint: Not yet. Ask: what had to happen before this?

slides.title: The power went out
slides.text: Read the story. Then trace the chain.

visual.text: A storm knocked down a tree. The tree hit a power line. The power went out at Kim's house. The fridge stopped working. The ice cream got soft. So Kim's family ate it all for dessert!

items.q: What knocked down the tree?
items.why: A storm knocked down the tree. That is the first cause.
items.no: Look at the first sentence.

items.q: The tree hit a power line. What did that cause?
items.why: Right after the tree hit the line, the power went out.
no: The storm came first. It is a cause, not this effect.
That happened at the very end.

items.q: The fridge stopped working. Is that a cause, an effect, or both? Type cause, effect or both.
items.why: The power going out caused it. It caused the soft ice cream. It is both.
items.no: Ask two questions: What caused it? What did it cause?

items.q: What was the last effect?
choices: The tree hit a power line.
items.why: Eating the ice cream is the end of the chain.
no: Soft ice cream caused one more thing.
That is in the middle of the chain.
That is near the start.

slides.title: Equal groups
slides.text:
Equal groups have the same number in each group.
Count the groups. Count in one group. Then multiply.
6 + 6 + 6 = 18, so 3 × 6 = 18.
slides.tip: Groups × how many in each group = the product.

slides.title: Grandpa's candle boxes
slides.text: Grandpa has 3 boxes. Each box has 7 candles. Make the groups.
slides.hint: Each box is one group. Set Groups to the number of boxes. Set In each group to the candles in one box.

items.q: Write 8 + 8 + 8 as multiplication: ____
items.no: Count the 8s. That is the number of groups.
Skip count by 5s. Touch each 5.

items.q: Which addition matches 2 × 6?
items.why: 2 × 6 is 2 groups of 6: 6 + 6 = 12.
no: 2 + 6 = 8. Two groups of 6 is 6 + 6.
That is three 2s, or 6.
That is three 6s, or 18.

items.q: This array has 3 rows of 8. How many carrots in all?
items.no: Skip count by 8s, one time for each row.

items.q: Which fact matches this array?
items.why: 4 rows with 2 in each row: 4 × 2 = 8.
no: 4 + 2 = 6. Count: there are 8 bottles.
There are 4 rows, not 2.
Each row has 2, not 4.

items.q: In an array, the things that go across make a ____.
items.why: Across ➡️ is a row. Up and down ⬇️ is a column.
items.no: Across is a r…. Up and down is a column.

slides.title: Shelf problems
slides.text: Are the groups equal? Then pick: multiply or add.

items.q: Mia puts 6 jars on each shelf. She fills 2 shelves. How many jars?
items.why: 2 groups of 6: 2 × 6 = 12.
items.no: Each shelf is a group. 6 + 6.

items.q: Theo has 4 bags of apples. The bags have 3, 5, 2 and 4 apples. How many apples?
items.why: The bags are not equal, so add: 3 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 14.
no: 4 × 3 = 12. But the bags are not equal! Add them.
4 × 4 = 16. But the bags are not equal! Add them.

items.q: Grandpa stacks 5 rows of logs. Each row has 5 logs. How many logs?
items.no: Skip count by 5s, one time for each row.

items.q: Round 68 to the nearest ten: ____
items.why: The ones digit is 8. 8 is 5 or more, so round up to 70.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. Is it 5 or more?

items.why: Regroup a ten: 12 − 8 = 4. Regroup a hundred: 12 − 6 = 6. 7 − 5 = 2. 264.
items.no: You can't take 8 from 2. Regroup first.

items.q: A story's setting tells ____.
choices: the problem the characters must solve
items.why: The setting is where and when a story happens.
no: Who is in the story are the characters.
The lesson is the theme.
The problem is the conflict.

sets.q: There are 4 crates. Each crate has 6 jugs. How many jugs?
sets.no: Each crate is a group. Skip count by 6s, once for each crate.

sets.q: Write 9 + 9 + 9 as multiplication: ____
sets.no: Count the 9s. That is the number of groups.

sets.q: Which fact matches this array of bread loaves?
sets.why: 3 rows with 5 in each row: 3 × 5 = 15.
no: 3 + 5 = 8. There are more than 8 loaves.
Count the rows. There are 3 rows, not 5.
Count again: 3 rows, 5 in each row.

sets.q: In 4 × 5 = 20, the 20 is called the ____.
sets.why: The answer when you multiply is the product.
sets.no: It is the answer to a times fact.

sets.q: The puppy chewed the shoe, so the shoe had holes. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
sets.why: Chewing is why the shoe had holes. It is the cause.
sets.no: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

sets.q:
Read: Dad forgot to close the window. Rain came in through the window. The rug got wet. The rug smelled bad.
What was the first cause?
choices: Rain came in through the window.
Dad forgot to close the window.
sets.why: It all started when Dad forgot to close the window.
no: The rug got wet because rain came in first.
Rain came in because of something before it.
That is the last effect.

sets.q: In the storm story, who boarded up the broken shutter?
sets.why: Theo boarded up the shutter. Mia found the cause.
sets.no: Mia found the problem. Who fixed it?

sets.q: A row of falling dominoes is a ____.
sets.why: Each domino knocks down the next one. That is a chain reaction.
no: The theme is the lesson of a story.
A character trait tells what a character is like.

sets.q: There are 5 boxes. Each box has 6 candles. How many candles?
sets.no: Each box is a group. Skip count by 6s, once for each box.

sets.q: Write 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 as multiplication: ____
sets.no: Count the 4s. That is the number of groups.

sets.q: Which fact matches this array of cheese blocks?
sets.why: 2 rows with 7 in each row: 2 × 7 = 14.
no: 2 + 7 = 9. Count: there are more than 9.
There are only 2 rows.
Each row has 7, not 2.

sets.q: Things set in equal rows and columns make an ____.
sets.why: Equal rows and columns make an array.
sets.no: It starts with a. Rows of cans on a shelf make one.

sets.q: Because it was cold, Rosa wore her coat. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
sets.why: Wearing the coat is what happened because it was cold. It is the effect.
sets.no: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

sets.q:
Read: Kai left his bike in the rain. The chain got rusty. The bike would not ride. Kai had to walk to school.
What was the last effect?
choices: Kai had to walk to school.
Kai left his bike in the rain.
sets.why: The chain ends with Kai had to walk to school. Nothing comes after it.
no: The rusty chain caused more things to happen.
A bike that won't ride caused one more thing.
That is the first cause.

sets.q: In the storm story, who traced the puddles back to the shutter?
sets.why: Mia traced the puddles back. Theo fixed the shutter.
sets.no: She found the puddles in the morning.

sets.q: The goods were ruined because the boxes got wet. A bad result of an action is a ____.
sets.why: A result, often a bad one, is a consequence.
no: A main character is a person in a story, not a result.
A cause is why something happens. Ruined goods are a result.

sets.q: There are 4 shelves. Each shelf has 7 cans. How many cans?
sets.no: Each shelf is a group. Add 7 four times: 7, 14, …

sets.q: Write 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 as multiplication: ____
sets.no: Count the 6s. That is the number of groups.

sets.q: Which fact matches this array of eggs?
sets.why: 3 rows with 6 in each row: 3 × 6 = 18.
no: 3 + 6 = 9. There are more than 9 eggs.
There are 3 rows, not 6.
Count the rows again. There are 3.

sets.q: Adding 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 is called repeated ____.
sets.why: Adding the same number again and again is repeated addition.
sets.no: You add the same number again and again. Repeated …

sets.q: Sam ate too fast, so he got a tummy ache. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
sets.why: The tummy ache is what happened. It is the effect.
sets.no: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

sets.q:
Read: The cat jumped on the shelf. A vase fell off. The vase broke. Grandma swept up the pieces.
Which event is both a cause and an effect?
choices: The cat jumped on the shelf.
sets.why: The vase broke because it fell. Then it made Grandma sweep. It does both jobs.
no: The cat jumping is the first cause. Nothing caused it in the story.
Sweeping is the last effect. It does not cause anything.

sets.q: In the storm story, the boxes got soaked. Then the wet boxes ____.
sets.why: The soaked boxes collapsed (fell down). Then the goods spilled.
sets.no: Think of the index cards: soaked, then …

sets.q: Mia followed the puddles back to the loose shutter. She ____ the chain.
sets.why: Following a chain back to the start is to trace it.
no: Multiply is a math word.
Rounding is a math word.
Ruined means spoiled. Mia did not spoil the chain.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Use counters or draw circles for the math. For the reading, ask why? and what happened next?

questions.q: There are 5 bowls. Each bowl has 2 peaches. How many peaches?
questions.no: Skip count by 2s, one time for each bowl.
Count the 7s. That is the number of groups.

no: 2 + 5 = 7. Count: there are 10 stars.
Each row has 5, not 2.
There are only 2 rows.

questions.q: Rae has 3 boxes of crayons. The boxes have 8, 8 and 6 crayons. How many crayons?
questions.why: The boxes are not equal, so add: 8 + 8 + 6 = 22.
no: 3 × 8 = 24, but one box has only 6.
3 × 6 = 18, but two boxes have 8.
8 + 6 = 14 leaves out one box.

questions.no: The product is the answer, after the = sign.

questions.q: Leo tripped on a toy, so he dropped his plate. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
questions.why: Tripping is why he dropped the plate. It is the cause.
questions.no: Ask: is the bold part why, or what happened?

questions.q: Because Gia practiced every day, she won the spelling bee. Is the bold part the cause or the effect? Type cause or effect.
questions.why: Winning is what happened because she practiced. It is the effect.
questions.no: Which happened first: practicing or winning?

visual.text: Tom left the milk out all day. The milk went sour. Tom could not eat his cereal for breakfast. He was hungry at school.

choices: Tom left the milk out all day.
Tom could not eat his cereal for breakfast.
questions.why: It all started when Tom left the milk out.
no: The milk went sour because of something that came before.
That is the last effect.
He could not eat cereal because the milk went sour.

questions.q: The milk went sour. Is that a cause, an effect, or both? Type cause, effect or both.

visual.text: Tom left the milk out all day. The milk went sour. Tom could not eat his cereal for breakfast. He was hungry at school.

questions.why: Leaving it out caused it. It caused no cereal. It is both.
questions.no: Ask two questions: What caused it? What did it cause?

questions.q: In the storm story, what was loose on the stockroom window?
questions.why: A loose shutter started the whole chain.
questions.no: It cracked in the wind. Theo boarded it up.

choices: a result of an action, often a bad one
the place and time where a story happens
the answer you get when you multiply
questions.why: A consequence is a result. It is often a bad one.
no: That is the setting.
That is the product.

teacher.objective: Ce'Line traces a cause-and-effect chain in a story: she finds the cause (why) and the effect (what happened), even when the cause comes after 'because', puts Mia's storm chain in order from the loose shutter to less inventory for opening day, and names middle events as both a cause and an effect. In math she connects equal groups, repeated addition and multiplication (4 groups of 5 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 4 × 5 = 20), reads arrays as rows × how many in each row, tells equal from unequal groups (multiply vs. add), and types the 10 Pathways Week 6 words (cause, effect, chain reaction, consequence, trace, multiply, equal groups, repeated addition, array, product).
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
About 40 counters (beans or cubes) and 6 small paper cups
10 index cards: 2 for CAUSE and EFFECT, 7 for the storm chain, 1 spare
Whiteboard and two marker colors, pencil
Packet (2 pages), printed for her to take home: page 1 is math, page 2 is reading

plan.do: Class slide 1. Two parts today: the storm story, then equal groups.
Class slide 2. Round 562, compare 507 and 570, 256 + 178 = 434, theme. She says each answer before she types.
Class slide 3. Take turns reading The Storm in the Stockroom aloud. Ask the three prompts. Check she knows inventory.
Class slide 4. Five cards: cause, effect, chain reaction, consequence, trace. She says each in her own words.
Class slide 5. Hold up the CAUSE and EFFECT cards. The musty smell: effect.
Class slide 6. She reads each sentence and asks both questions. Watch the 'because' sentences.
Class slide 7. She writes the 7 events on index cards, lines them up with arrows, then taps the order.
Class slide 8. Touch the 'soaked' card, then the card before and after it. Middle events are both.
Class slide 9. Kayla's crayons: she draws the chain with arrows on the whiteboard, then answers.
Class slide 10 on her own: Mia, Theo, a loose shutter, trace.
Class slide 11. Five cards. She spells array and product out loud.
Class slide 12. 5 cups with 3 counters each. Skip count by 3s to 15, then build it on screen.
Class slide 13. Whiteboard: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 under 4 × 5. Circle the groups and how many in each.
Class slide 14. Counters or circles for each. Jo's bags: not equal, so add.
Class slide 15. She builds 4 rows of 6 counters, skip counts by 6s, then turns the paper: 6 rows of 4, still 24.
Class slide 16. She touches each row and skip counts: 18, 5 × 3, 12.
Class slide 17 on her own: 18 boxes, product, 16 packets, 6 × 3. Note her first answers.
Class slide 18. Open the course page and read the task list with her, one line at a time. Hand her the printed packet.

watch: Cause after 'because': in 'The milk spilled because the cup tipped over', the cause is the SECOND part. If she picks whatever comes first in the sentence, ask: which happened first in time?
First cause in Mia's story: Pathways wants 'a loose shutter'. If she says 'the puddles' (what Mia saw first) or 'rain got inside', trace it back with the index cards.
Middle events: she may call a middle event only a cause or only an effect. Have her ask both questions: what caused it? what did it cause? If both have answers, it is both.
Mia and Theo: Pathways asks who led the investigation (Mia) and who boarded up the shutter (Theo). Say: Mia found it, Theo fixed it.
Adding the factors: 3 × 4 = 7 means she added the two numbers. Build it with cups and counters: 3 cups, 4 in each.
Counting by ones: if she counts every counter one by one, model the skip count once (3, 6, 9 …) and have her touch each cup as she says it.
Groups vs. how many in each: for 6 + 6 + 6 she should say 'three 6s, 3 × 6'. 6 × 3 is accepted everywhere (same product), but the words 'groups of' must match.
Unequal groups: if she multiplies when the bags have different numbers (Jo, Theo, Rae), ask: does every bag have the same number? If not, add.
Arrays: rows go across. If she counts columns as rows, run a finger along one row and say 'this is one row'.
Typing words: product, array, consequence and trace are typed in Pathways. Watch spelling (prodct, arry, consequense).

teacher.notes: For you only: this lesson is one Pathways week (Week 6: Stocking the Shelves and The Storm in the Stockroom), the first week of Pathways Unit 2. The math is the introduction to multiplication (equal groups, repeated addition, arrays, product); the facts stay small (products up to 30) so she can focus on the idea and on skip counting. The reading skill is cause-and-effect chains in the Pathways storm story. The class lesson uses the real storm chain because Pathways Week 6 Reading asks about it (first cause, last effect, who traced it, who fixed the shutter); the after-class lesson, Practice and Show What You Know use new KCE stories and new numbers. Show What You Know has 8 questions (4 math, 4 reading; 3 different sets for retakes; she needs 85, so 7 of 8). The holidays: the next lesson is Lesson 7 on Tue, Dec 29 (you are away Dec 20–28). Her task list is light and spread over two weeks: the week before Christmas (after-class lesson, Practice, Packet page 1, Pathways Week 6 Reading) and Christmas week (Packet page 2, Pathways Week 6 Math). She brings packet page 2 to the Dec 29 lesson. The Winter holiday lesson, Science Week 6 and Social Studies Week 6 are optional and not taught. Both Pathways lessons ask for a printed Pre/Post sheet; print it for her if she has no printer at home. Next lesson: Tue, Dec 29. Start it by checking her packet and her Pathways Week 6 scores. If she is under 85 on Show What You Know, open the Formspree missed list: a missed equal-groups or array item means 5 minutes with cups and counters (groups × how many in each, then skip count); a missed 'add or multiply' item means sorting equal and unequal bags; a missed cause/effect item means the 'why? / what happened?' questions with the CAUSE and EFFECT cards; a missed story item means retelling the storm chain with the index cards (keep them for Dec 29). If either Pathways Week 6 lesson is under 85, she retakes it in that lesson with you.
